rows.w: A 133-hectare island off Punggol, once owned by the Aw brothers of Tiger Balm. In 1950 it was sold to a businessman who planned a resort modelled on New York's Coney Island. Since October 2015 a 50-hectare NParks park has kept it deliberately rustic: casuarina woods, a 2.5 km car-free trail, hidden beaches and bridges at both ends to the mainland.

A National Heritage Board historic site. On 23 February 1942, during the Japanese Sook Ching operation, a Hojo Kempei firing squad killed some 300–400 Chinese civilians on the Punggol foreshore. Human remains turned up in the sand in 1977 and 1997. An NHB marker set up in 1995, for the 50th anniversary of the end of WWII, records the killings.

The 4.2-km park along Singapore's longest man-made waterway, in four themed zones (Nature Cove, Recreation Zone, Heritage Zone on Old Punggol Road, Green Gallery) linked by five photogenic bridges — the dome-shaped Jewel Bridge for sunsets over the Punggol and Serangoon reservoirs, the snaking red Sunrise Bridge at the eastern Sunrise Gateway, plus the Wave, Adventure and Kelong bridges. Otters are regulars.

rows.w: CLOSED 2 May 2024. The seafood restaurant that carried the old 'Ponggol' spelling and the memory of the kelong-era Punggol seafood strip — in business since 1965, famous for chilli crab, lala bee hoon and mee goreng (Honeycombers) — quietly shut after 55 years (Seth Lui). Kept, flagged, as part of Punggol's food history.

rows.n: Sixth Floor Oyster Cake (Northshore Plaza) — CLOSED
rows.w: A Punggol home business (named for the owner's sixth-floor HDB flat) that grew into a Northshore Plaza kiosk frying ultra-crisp Fuzhou oyster cakes — two whole oysters, minced meat and shrimp — covered by Eatbook and Women's Weekly. CLOSED: both outlets shut permanently after 28 Sep 2025 (Seth Lui).
